catalog_quote: [sec. 2.1.2 Tones, p. 7] As in other Dogon languages, there are two tone levels. Using angled brackets for single-syllabic contoured tones, syllables are H, L, <HL>, <LH>, and infrequently bell-shaped <LHL>. ... L:exical [sic] tone melodies for non-verb stems are similar: /H/, /L/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/, plus one noun stem (likely a borrowing) with /HLH/ ... [sec. 3.1.2 Metrical structure, p. 13] In the sequence CvCvCv, the medial syllable from the left may be metrically weak. This is most evident in some types of trisyllabic verbs, whose second vowel is a short high vowel (§10.2.3.1). It may also be at work in syncope (§3.5.3.4) and truncation (§3.5.4.7) in suffixed /CvCv-Cv/ derivatives of verb stems. [sec. 8.4.7.5, p. 217] Rwo [sic] examples in (282g) are straightforward derivational iterations of input verbs. I found some fluctuation between H.L.L-H.L.L and H.H.H-L.L.L tones in these cases. Given the stress attack on the first syllable of H.H.H and of L.L.L words, H.L.L-H.L.L and H.H.H-L.L.L are difficult to distinguish. [sec. 10.2.3.1, p. 278] In CvCvCv-, the medial syllable is generally in a weak metrical position in Dogon languages, and the high vowel can be thought of as reflecting this.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yanda Dom is described as a tone language (lexical tone melodies plus grammatical overlays); stress is not treated as a phonological category. The only statements bearing on prominence are (i) an incidental remark that level-toned (all-H or all-L) words have a phonetic 'stress attack' on their first syllable, and (ii) that the medial syllable of CvCvCv is metrically weak (vowel raising/syncope site), i.e. word-initial prominence, non-contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the p. 217 remark is limited to H.H.H and L.L.L (level-toned) words; metrical weakness of the medial syllable is hedged ('may be metrically weak').
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level; remark made in the context of iterated (reduplicative) expressive adverbials where H.L.L-H.L.L vs H.H.H-L.L.L tone patterns are hard to tell apart. No phrase-level stress discussed; intonation (sec. 3.8) covers only prolongation and 'dying-quail' contour.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Yanda Dom proper (yàndá-dòm), villages of Upper/Lower Yanda, Ogol cluster and Ana(na), eastern cliffs of the Dogon plateau near Bamba, Mali = Glottolog yand1257 / ISO dym. Heath notes two assistants with minor tonal differences (second assistant merges two verb tone classes). The other three Glottolog 'descriptive refs' listed for yand1257 (Bunoge, Yorno So, Donno So grammars) describe different Dogon languages and are mis-associated.

sources.note: Treats YD as a tone language (ch. 3.7 Tones, pp. 58-91; lexical melodies /H/,/L/,/LH/,/HL/,/LHL/ plus grammatical overlays). No dedicated stress/accent section; 'accent' never used. Sec. 3.1.2 'Metrical structure' (p. 13): in CvCvCv the medial syllable may be metrically weak (evidence: high-vowel reduction, syncope). One incidental remark p. 217 (sec. 8.4.7.5): 'Given the stress attack on the first syllable of H.H.H and of L.L.L words, H.L.L-H.L.L and H.H.H-L.L.L are difficult to distinguish.'

sources.note: Dogon NP tonosyntax arose from the interlocking of (a) a right-headed prosodic pattern in noun-modifier sequences, (b) loss of numeral classifiers that had protected nouns before numerals, and (c) transfer of tones from possessors to following possessums; the resulting system was reinterpreted semantically and is diachronically stable (tonogenesis-of-grammatical-tone analysis, not a synchronic YD tone inventory).

sources.note: Lexical tone melodies of words and word strings in Dogon languages are overridden by syntactically conditioned word-level or broader tone overlays; NP-internal reference restrictors (possessors, adjectives, relative clauses, demonstratives) are controllers imposing overlays such as {L} and {HL} on adjacent targets, while nonsingular quantifiers and discourse-functional morphemes are not; overlays are sensitive to controller edge tone, prosodic weight of the target and linear adjacency.
